html:
Senegal is the westernmost country of mainland Africa, named after the Senegal River, and independent since 1960. The map shows a Senegal from 1530 onward: first the Wolof and Serer kingdoms and the European trading posts on their coast, then the French colony and the modern state.

Before 1550 most of the land was ruled by the Jolof Empire. It broke up into the kingdoms of Kayor, Baol, Waalo, Sine and Saloum, while Futa Toro, the old land of Takrur, held the river valley.

Europeans traded along this coast from the 1440s:

  • France founded Saint-Louis at the river mouth in 1659.
  • The island of Gorée off Cape Verde changed hands between the Dutch, British and French and became a base for the Atlantic slave trade and for trade in gum arabic.
  • In the 1850s Governor Louis Faidherbe pushed French rule inland, and groundnuts became the main cash crop.

Senegal became the core of French West Africa, with Dakar as its capital from 1902. People born in the Four Communes of Saint-Louis, Gorée, Rufisque and Dakar had French citizenship and elected a deputy to Paris.

The poet Léopold Sédar Senghor led Senegal to independence in 1960 and was president for twenty years. Unlike most of its neighbours, Senegal has never had a military coup, and power has changed hands through elections since 2000.
